look_here_first: Go straight to the leaf's deep middle sinuses and the acorn cup: bur oak often has a broad fiddle-shaped leaf with a narrow waist, and the huge cup wraps much of the nut with a conspicuously fringed or 'mossy' rim.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Kew/POWO accepts Quercus macrocarpa and lists Texas in its native range. Hays County — the project Hays County native-source list (Wildflower Center printable list compiled/managed by NPSOT Hill Country Chapter) includes Q. macrocarpa. Bell County — Fort Cavazos identifies Bur oak as native to the installation. Williamson County — a county archaeological/environmental survey describes historical bottomland forests containing Q. macrocarpa.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Purola Preserve separately lists its Q. macrocarpa occurrence as introduced at that site, so that local planted occurrence is not used as Hays native evidence.

best_field_traits: large leaves often broadest toward tip with deep middle sinuses creating a waist
upper blade often shallowly lobed beyond the deep middle sinuses
cupule commonly encloses one-half or more of nut and bears long soft fringe around rim
morphology_keys.oak_training: Use leaf architecture plus bark/twig/buds and mature acorn/cupule; never identify an oak from leaf silhouette alone.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Quercus muehlenbergii: Chinkapin oak has chestnut-like regularly toothed leaves and a non-fringed bowl-like cup; bur oak has deep midleaf sinuses and the diagnostic mossy/fringed cup. Quercus alba: White oak has regular rounded lobes down the blade and a shallow non-fringed cup; bur oak's middle sinuses and oversized fringed cup are decisive. Quercus lyrata: Overcup oak has a cup that can nearly enclose the nut but lacks bur oak's characteristic long mossy fringe and differs in leaf form.

photo_note: Required diagnostic roles include leaf upper/lower surface, bark, twig/buds, mature acorn and cupule; photo polish may continue after install.
